questions.q: What operationally characterizes the NISQ era, as defined in the lesson?
options: Running arbitrarily long and deep circuits reliably using continuous below-threshold error correction
A regime where every quantum computer already uses the surface code at distance 27 or higher
Running circuits with no error correction, or only small-scale demonstration-level error correction, limiting usable algorithms to shallow, noise-tolerant, or classically-checkable ones
A purely theoretical era that no real hardware has ever actually occupied
questions.explain: NISQ-era hardware lacks full error correction, so it is restricted to algorithm classes that can tolerate accumulated noise -- shallow circuits, variational methods, or classically post-selectable outputs.

questions.q: What would the fault-tolerant era require operationally, beyond simply having more physical qubits?
options: Nothing beyond raw qubit count -- qubit count alone determines fault tolerance
Only a faster classical computer to run alongside the quantum hardware

A full stack operating together continuously: a workable-threshold code, fault-tolerant gadgets for every operation including error correction itself, a complete universal gate set, and a decoder fast enough to keep pace
Simply running NISQ-era algorithms for a longer period of time
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that fault tolerance requires the full integrated stack -- code, gadgets, gate set, and decoder -- operating continuously, not just a larger qubit count.

questions.q: What is the lesson's central, explicit honesty claim about the current state of the field?
options: The transition to fault tolerance is purely a software problem with no remaining hardware challenges
NISQ-era hardware has already been fully replaced by fault-tolerant hardware
As of now, no quantum computer has run a classically-infeasible, practically useful algorithm end-to-end in the fault-tolerant regime
Fault-tolerant quantum computing was achieved as of this course's writing
questions.explain: This is stated directly as the course's explicit checkpoint claim -- no useful, classically-infeasible algorithm has yet been run end-to-end in the fault-tolerant regime.

questions.q: Why does the lesson caution against describing the transition to fault tolerance as 'almost done' or 'right around the corner'?
options: Because the course wants to discourage people from studying quantum computing
Because no further research is being conducted in this area at all
Because fault tolerance has actually already been fully achieved, making the caution unnecessary
The gap between current demonstrations and what's needed is measured in orders of magnitude of physical-qubit count, a genuinely hard multi-decade engineering problem, not a minor remaining step
questions.explain: Chapter 6's resource-estimation math shows the gap in physical-qubit terms is enormous (hundreds to tens of millions), which is why the lesson insists on calling this an open, hard engineering challenge rather than a nearly-finished one.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that being able to precisely distinguish demonstrated milestones from the remaining fault-tolerance gap is a valuable skill?
options: Because quantum computing journalism is always perfectly accurate and requires no critical evaluation
Because the field includes plenty of enthusiasm, funding pitches, and press coverage that blur this line, and precise understanding is a differentiating skill
Because the distinction is purely academic and has no practical relevance to anyone working in the field
Because no one else in the field understands this distinction
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this precise, honest framing as valuable specifically because real-world communication about the field often blurs the line between demonstrated progress and remaining challenges.
